exercises.name: Hip hinge
exercises.description: Hip Hinge Exercise DescriptionThe hip hinge is a fundamental movement pattern that involves bending at the hips while keeping the spine neutral. It is commonly used in exercises like deadlifts, kettlebell swings, and good mornings. To perform a hip hinge:    Starting Position: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and a slight bend in your knees.    Hinge at the Hips: Push your hips back while maintaining a straight back. Your torso should lean forward, and your chest should stay up.    Lowering Phase: Continue to hinge until your torso is nearly parallel to the ground, or until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings.    Return to Standing: Drive through your heels and thrust your hips forward to return to the starting position.

performed on the Smith machine, ideal for targeting the legs and glutes.

body until the front thigh is parallel to the ground while the bar
slides vertically along the machine. This exercise helps improve
stability, correct muscle imbalances, and reduces stress on the back,
providing a safe environment for strength training.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Scaption
exercises.description:
Starting position:

Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart.

Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip (palms facing each other).

Keep a slight bend in your elbows, shoulders relaxed and shoulder blades pulled back.

Execution:

Slowly raise the dumbbells forward and slightly to the side, at about a 30–45° angle from your body (between a front raise and a lateral raise).

Lift until your arms are about shoulder height (do not go overhead).

Pause for a second at the top and feel the activation in your shoulders and scapular stabilizers.

Lower the dumbbells back down under control to the starting position.

Breathing:

Inhale as you lower the dumbbells.

Exhale as you lift them.

Common mistakes:

Using dumbbells that are too heavy (causing jerky movements).

Lifting above shoulder height (puts unnecessary stress on the shoulder joint).

Arching the lower back instead of keeping the movement controlled at the shoulders.

Purpose of the exercise:

Activates the lower trapezius, serratus anterior, and scapular stabilizers.

Helps correct posture and improve shoulder balance.

exercises.name: Sliding Lateral Lunge
exercises.description: Stand upright with your feet hip-width apart, holding a kettlebell close to your chest in goblet position. Place one foot on a slider, gliding disc, or towel. Keep your chest tall and core engaged. Slowly slide the foot outward to the side while bending the opposite knee, lowering your hips into a lateral lunge. Keep the working leg’s knee aligned with the toes and avoid letting it collapse inward. The non-working leg remains straight and slides smoothly along the floor. Push through the heel of the bent leg to return to the starting position while maintaining control of the kettlebell.

exercises.name: Arm Raises (T/Y/I)
exercises.description:
Stand upright with feet hip-width apart, core engaged, and arms relaxed at your sides. From this position, perform three different arm raises to target the shoulders and upper back:

T Raise: Lift your arms straight out to the sides until they are parallel to the floor, forming a “T” shape.

Y Raise: Lift your arms upward at about a 45° angle from your body to form a “Y” shape.

I Raise: Raise your arms straight overhead, close together, forming an “I” shape.

Maintain a neutral spine, avoid arching your lower back, and move slowly with control. Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together and keeping your shoulders down away from your ears.

exercises.name: Typewriter Pull-ups
exercises.description: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, slightly wider than shoulder-width. Pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar. At the top position, instead of going straight down, shift your body to one side by extending one arm while keeping the other arm bent. Move smoothly from one side to the other, like a typewriter motion, before lowering yourself back down. This exercise increases time under tension and strengthens the lats, biceps, and shoulders while building unilateral pulling strength.

exercises.name: Bodyweight Biceps Curl
exercises.description: Set up under a straight bar (around waist or chest height). Grip the bar with your palms facing you (supinated grip), hands about shoulder-width apart. Lean back with straight arms so that your body is at an angle to the ground. Keeping your elbows high and close to the bar, pull your upper body toward the bar by flexing your elbows, similar to a biceps curl. Lower yourself back down in a controlled manner. Keep your core tight and movement slow to maximize tension on the biceps.

exercises.name: Treadmill Cardio
exercises.description:
It's a cardiovascular workout performed on a treadmill to improve endurance, burn calories, and promote heart health. It offers multiple benefits, such as the ability to easily adjust speed and incline, allowing for a variety of workouts, from hill walking to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and tempo runs. To optimize results, it's important to vary your workouts.
Benefits of Treadmill Cardio:

Improved Cardiovascular Health:
Regular aerobic exercise on a treadmill strengthens the heart and lungs, which can help prevent heart disease.

Weight Loss:
By burning calories, treadmill training can be an effective tool for weight loss and maintaining a healthy weight.

Muscle Strengthening:
It strengthens the muscles in the legs and glutes, helping to prevent muscle loss, which is especially important with age.

Training Flexibility:
Allows you to vary speed, incline, and intervals, making your workout more dynamic and adaptable to different fitness levels.
Types of Treadmill Training:

Hill Walking:
Increasing the incline of the treadmill and walking at a brisk pace can improve endurance and work your leg muscles.

Endurance Jog:
A run at a comfortable, steady pace that keeps your heart rate in a target zone (such as Zone 2) to build endurance.

Interval Training:
Alternating periods of high intensity (fast running) with periods of low intensity (easy walking or jogging) to maximize calorie burn and cardiovascular improvement.

Tempo Run:
A run at a steady, sustained pace that is slightly faster than a normal jog, which challenges your ability to sustain a more intense effort for an extended period.

exercises.name: Dumbbell donkey kick
exercises.description:
The dumbbell donkey kick is an effective exercise for working the glute and hamstring muscles. This exercise is usually performed on all fours, using a dumbbell to add resistance. The steps for performing it correctly are described below.
Starting position: Get on all fours on a mat, with your hands aligned under your shoulders and your knees aligned under your hips.
Placing the dumbbell: Take a dumbbell and place it behind the knee of the leg you are going to lift. Make sure it is held securely to prevent it from falling during the exercise.
Exercise:
Inhale and, as you exhale, lift the leg with the dumbbell upward, keeping the knee bent at a 90-degree angle.
Raise the leg until it is parallel to the floor, feeling the contraction in the glutes.
Hold the position for one second at the top and then slowly lower the leg back to the starting position.
Repetitions: Perform 10 to 15 repetitions per leg, making sure to maintain good form throughout the exercise.
Sets: Complete 2 to 3 sets, depending on your fitness level.

exercises.name: Stationary bike cardio
exercises.description:
Benefits of Stationary Bike Cardio
Stationary bike cardio is an excellent form of exercise that offers multiple benefits for health and well-being. Here are some of the most notable ones:
Improved Cardiovascular Health
Strengthens the heart: Regular exercise helps improve the heart's efficiency and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Increases circulation: It improves blood flow, which can help lower blood pressure.
Calorie Burning and Weight Loss
Efficient for burning calories: Depending on the intensity, you can burn between 400 and 600 calories per hour.
Helps with weight loss: Combined with a balanced diet, stationary bike cardio can be effective for losing weight.
Muscle Strengthening
Tones the legs: It mainly works the leg muscles, including the quadriceps, hamstrings and calves.
Improves muscular endurance: Over time, you can increase the endurance and strength in your legs.
Mental Health Benefits
Reduces stress: Exercise releases endorphins, which can improve your mood and reduce stress.
Boosts energy: Regular physical activity can raise your energy levels and improve sleep quality.

exercises.name: Weighted Crunch
exercises.description:
The Weighted Crunch is a variation of the classic crunch exercise that involves adding resistance (a weight) to increase the intensity of the abdominal work.

Lay down

(Optional) Bend your knees to add difficulty

(Optional) Bend your knees and let your feet rest on a bench or a box or something (90 degree angle on knees)

Lift your head and torso while bending your back forward (if you don't it's a sit-up and also involves some back muscles). The higher you go, the more you should feel your abs contracting.

Go back to starting position an repeat

exercises.name: Seated Hip Abduction
exercises.description:
Starting Position:

Adjust the seat height so that your knees are aligned with the pivot point of the machine.

Sit with your back flat against the backrest, maintaining good posture.

Place the outside of your thighs against the machine's padded levers.

Position your feet flat on the footrests or platform of the machine.

Grasp the handles or sides of the seat for stability.

Ensure your spine is neutral and your core is slightly engaged.

Movement:

Exhale as you slowly push your legs outward against the resistance pads.

Focus on initiating the movement from your hips, not your knees.

Continue opening your legs until you feel a strong contraction in your outer hips and thighs.

Hold the fully abducted position briefly (1-2 seconds) to maximize muscle engagement.

Inhale as you slowly control the return of your legs to the starting position, resisting the weight throughout the movement.

Avoid allowing the weight stack to touch down between repetitions to maintain constant tension on the muscles.

Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control throughout the set.

exercises.name: Cable Fly Upper Chest
exercises.description:
Execution

Start position:

Arms down and slightly behind your body, elbows slightly bent.

Feel a light stretch across your chest.

Movement:

Bring your hands upward and together in front of your upper chest — roughly at chin to collarbone level.

Use a smooth, controlled motion (avoid jerking).

Squeeze your chest at the top for 1–2 seconds.

Return:

Slowly let your arms move back down and out to the sides, keeping control and tension.

exercises.name: Cable Fly Lower Chest
exercises.description:
Execution

Start position:

Arms extended out to your sides in a “Y” shape.

Feel a stretch in your chest (slight bend in elbows — don’t lock them).

Movement:

Bring your hands downward and together in front of your lower chest or upper abs, in a smooth arc motion.

Squeeze your chest hard at the bottom for 1–2 seconds.

Return:

Slowly raise your arms back up along the same path until you feel a good stretch in your chest.

Maintain control — don’t let the weights pull you back too quickly.

exercises.name: Incline Static Hold
exercises.description:
Execution

Hold Position:

Lower the dumbbells a few inches above your chest — about the midpoint of a normal incline press.

This is where your upper chest is under maximum tension.

Static Hold:

Hold the position for 20–45 seconds while keeping the chest tight.

Breathe slowly but stay tense — do not relax your chest or shoulders.

End the set:

After the hold, carefully bring the dumbbells down and rest.

exercises.name: Flat Machine Press
exercises.description:
Execution

Start position:

Elbows bent at roughly 90°, hands just outside your chest.

Keep wrists straight and aligned with your forearms.

Pressing phase (concentric):

Push the handles forward until your arms are almost fully extended — don’t lock out.

Focus on squeezing your chest at the end of the movement.

Returning phase (eccentric):

Slowly bring the handles back toward your chest, feeling the stretch in your pecs.

Maintain tension — don’t let the weight stack touch down between reps.

exercises.name: Tuck L-sit
exercises.description: The tuck L-sit is a bodyweight hold where you support yourself on parallel bars, parallettes, or the floor with straight arms while pulling your knees toward your chest. Your hips stay lifted, your spine stays tall, and your feet hover off the ground. The goal is to keep your core tight, shoulders depressed, and arms locked out while maintaining the tucked position. It’s a core-intensive, shoulder-stabilizing static hold often used as a progression toward the full L-sit.

Preparation: Stand with your feet together. Hold the kettlebell with both hands by the handle, keeping it close to your chest, or hold it with one hand (on the same side as the working leg).

exercises.name: Single-leg side glute press
exercises.description:
The Single-Leg Side Glute Press is a leg press machine variation where you angle your body sideways on the pad, placing one foot high and slightly angled to press the weight, powerfully targeting the outer glute (gluteus medius/minimus) and hamstrings for balanced leg development and stability, requiring focus on pushing through the heel and maintaining control without locking out.

How to Perform:

Setup: Sit in the leg press machine, rotate your body to one hip, placing one foot high on the platform at about a 45-degree angle with toes pointed slightly out/forward.

Positioning: Keep your hip, knee, and ankle aligned, and ensure your lower back stays on the pad.

Descent: Slowly lower the weight, allowing your knee to bend deeply (near 90 degrees), feeling a stretch in your glute and hamstring.

Press: Drive through your heel (not your toes) to press the weight back up, squeezing your glutes and hamstrings, stopping just before your leg fully extends.

Control: Avoid bouncing and don't let your lower back lift off the pad; maintain tension throughout the movement.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Deadlift with Dumbbell
exercises.description:
Starting Position: Stand upright with a slight bend in your knees, holding a dumbbell in one or both hands. Shift your weight onto your supporting leg (e.g., your right leg) and lift your non-supporting foot slightly off the floor.

The Hinge: Keeping your back flat and core engaged, hinge at your hips, pushing your glutes backward. As your torso lowers, extend your non-supporting leg straight back behind you for balance, keeping your hips square to the floor. The dumbbell(s) should lower toward the ground along the line of your supporting leg.

Range of Motion: Continue lowering your torso until it is nearly parallel to the floor, or you feel an intense stretch in your supporting hamstring, ensuring your back remains neutral throughout the movement.

Return to Start: Pause at the bottom, then contract your glutes and hamstrings to slowly raise your torso back to the starting position. Your non-supporting leg should return in line with the supporting one.

Switch Sides: After completing your desired number of repetitions on one side, switch your weight and repeat the movement on the other leg.

exercises.name: Machine Side Lateral Raises
exercises.description:
Machine side lateral raises are an isolation exercise for the side (lateral) deltoids, performed on a machine for stability, targeting the outer shoulder by lifting pads or handles out to the sides to shoulder height, then lowering slowly, keeping elbows slightly bent and traps down to focus on the delts. This exercise helps build shoulder width by preventing swinging and providing constant tension, making it great for beginners or as a finisher.

How to Perform Machine Lateral Raises

Setup: Adjust the seat so your shoulders align with the machine's pivot point, your chest is against the pad (or back if facing out), and your arms are at a 90-degree angle with the pads/handles.

Starting Position: Grip the handles with a relaxed grip, elbows slightly bent, and shoulders down (depressed) away from your ears.

Lifting Phase: Exhale and lift your arms out to the sides, moving your upper arms laterally, until they are parallel to the floor.

Peak Contraction: Pause briefly at the top, squeezing the side delts, but don't shrug your shoulders up.

Lowering Phase: Inhale and slowly lower the weight back down with control, resisting the weight on the way down.

exercises.name: Cable Front Raise with a small bar
exercises.description:
The Cable Front Raise with a small bar isolates your anterior deltoids (front shoulders) by providing constant tension, requiring you to stand facing away from a low pulley, grab the bar with an overhand grip, and lift it in front of you to shoulder height with slightly bent arms, avoiding swinging and keeping your core tight for controlled movement up and down. Use a light-to-moderate weight, focusing on slow, controlled reps to feel the muscle work, not momentum.

How to Perform the Cable Front Raise (Bar)

Setup: Attach a small straight bar to a low cable pulley. Set the weight to a light or moderate setting.

Starting Position: Stand with your back to the machine, holding the bar with an overhand grip (palms facing down) at hip level, arms extended but not locked. Feet shoulder-width apart, core braced, shoulders back and down.

The Lift: Exhale and slowly raise the bar straight up in front of you, keeping a slight bend in your elbows, until your hands reach shoulder height (or slightly below).

The Hold: Pause briefly at the top, squeezing your front delts.

The Lower: Inhale as you slowly and controllably lower the bar back to the starting position, maintaining tension.

exercises.name: Smith machine squat
exercises.description:
Technique and Execution

The Smith machine squat is a variation of the traditional barbell squat that uses a guided, fixed-path barbell. Here's a detailed breakdown of the proper technique:

Starting Position

Foot Placement: Position feet slightly forward of the bar, about shoulder-width apart

Bar Position: Rest the bar on your upper trapezius/shoulders, similar to a traditional back squat

Stance: Feet can be slightly angled outward for natural hip rotation

Squat Movement

Unrack the bar by rotating it to release from the safety hooks

Slowly lower your body by bending knees and hips

Descend until thighs are parallel to the ground (or slightly below)

Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement

Drive through your heels to return to the starting position

Benefits and Considerations

Advantages

Reduced Balance Requirements: Fixed bar path makes it easier for beginners

Controlled Movement: Less risk of improper form compared to free weight squats

Isolation: Allows focused leg muscle development

exercises.name: Machine Hip Abduction
exercises.description:
Technique and Execution

Starting Position

Seated Positioning: Sit in the machine with back against the pad

Leg Placement: Inner thighs against the machine's padded resistance points

Adjust Machine: Set seat position to align your hip joint with the machine's pivot point

Movement Technique

Start with legs together or slightly pressed against the inner pads

Slowly push legs outward, spreading them apart

Move until maximum comfortable lateral range is reached

Pause briefly at the outer point of the movement

Slowly return to the starting position with controlled movement

Biomechanical Breakdown

Muscle Engagement

Primary Activation: Gluteus Medius (side hip muscle)

Stabilization: Engages core and lower back muscles

Functional Movement: Mimics lateral leg movement used in walking, sports, and daily activities

Benefits

Strength and Stability

Improves Hip Stability

Reduces Risk of Knee Injuries

Enhances Lateral Movement Capabilities

Targets Often-Neglected Muscle Groups

exercises.name: Cable pull through
exercises.description:
The Cable Pull Through is a lower-body exercise that targets the glutes and hamstrings using a "hip hinge" motion. To perform it, attach a rope to the lowest pulley setting, face away from the machine with the rope between your legs, and step forward to create tension. Keeping your back flat and knees slightly soft, push your hips backward as if trying to close a door behind you until you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings.

To finish the rep, explosively drive your hips forward to return to a standing position, squeezing your glutes hard at the top. It is vital to remember that this is not a squat; your knees should not bend deeply, and your arms should remain straight and relaxed, acting only as hooks for the rope. This movement provides constant tension on the glutes while placing less stress on the lower back than a traditional deadlift.

exercises.name: Barbell Full Squat
exercises.description:
The barbell full squat is a compound exercise that targets multiple muscle groups in the lower body, including the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.

Proper form is crucial for maximizing results and preventing injuries during the barbell full squat. This includes maintaining a shoulder-width stance, creating whole body tension, controlling your descent, and maintaining proper depth and knee positioning.

Assistance moves such as the front squat, goblet squat, split squat, and Bulgarian split squat can help improve your performance in the barbell full squat by targeting specific muscle groups and improving overall technique.

To achieve new personal records in your back squat, gradually increase weight over time, vary rep ranges and sets to stimulate muscle growth, and prioritize rest and recovery between training sessions.

exercises.name: Open Book
exercises.description:
Basic exercise

Focus: enhances thoracic mobility and
spinal segmentation while opening the shoulders and chest.

**Position:**kneeling on the floor with your right side facing a wall. Hips are square and stable, with the right knee down and the left foot forward. Lengthen your spine and align your head comfortably.
Begin with your arms relaxed and open in front of your chest, palms
facing each other and hands apart.

Inhale
to initiate the movement, allowing your left arm —the one farther from
the wall— to open outward and backward. Lead the twist from your thoracic
spine, rotating your upper back progressively while keeping your pelvis
still.

Exhale as you complete the rotation, guiding your left hand
toward the wall as your gaze follows your hand.

Return by inhaling and
slowly bringing your arm forward, reversing the spinal rotation segment
by segment.

Repeat on the opposite side.

Progression

**Position:**kneeling on the floor with your right side facing a wall. Left knee down and right foot forward.

Before the basic exercise: inhale, exhalewhile moving the right arm along the wall with a circle upwards and backwards, inhalewhile bringing back the arm.

Basic exercise.

Repeat on the opposite side.

exercises.name: Dumbell Tate Press
exercises.description:
Set Up: Lie flat with a dumbbell in each hand. Extend your arms straight up over your chest as if you were at the top of a dumbbell bench press

Starting Position: Position the dumbbells so they are touching or very close together with a pronated grip (palms facing your feet and thumbs facing each other)

Lowering: Without moving your upper arms or shoulders, bend your elbows and flare them outward to the sides. Lower the inner ends of the dumbbells toward the center of your chest

Touch and Pause: Gently touch the dumbbells to your chest. Do not rest the weight on your body; maintain constant tension in your triceps

Press: Forcefully extend your elbows to return the dumbbells to the starting position. Focus on "pushing your pinkies toward the sky" to maximize triceps engagement

exercises.name: Band pull-apart with external rotation
exercises.description:
Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, chest out, and shoulders back.

Hold the resistance band with both hands, palms facing up or facing each other, depending on the band type.

Bend your elbows at a 90-degree angle and glue your upper arms to your sides.

The band should have some tension in the starting position, with your hands closer together in front of your stomach.

Rotate Outward: While keeping your elbows tucked into your sides, slowly move your hands away from each other, stretching the band.

Squeeze: Squeeze your shoulder blades together and down as you rotate your hands outward.

Range of Motion: Rotate your hands as far outward as you comfortably can without allowing your elbows to leave your sides.

Hold: Hold the end position for 1–2 seconds to maximize muscle engagement.

Return: Slowly and with control, bring your hands back to the starting position.

exercises.description:
Lie on your back with knees and hips bent at 90 degrees (tabletop).

Hold for 10 seconds of maximum effort. Your abs should be shaking.

exercises.name: Landmine Squat to Press
exercises.description:
Bar Position: Anchor one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or a secure corner.
Stance: Stand facing the barbell with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width. Turn your toes out 10–35 degrees to allow for better pelvic movement and depth.
Grip: Cup the free end of the barbell with both hands (fingers interlaced or overlapping) and hold it at mid-chest level, just below the collarbone.

Descent: Brace your core and sit back into a squat, keeping your chest up and weight on your heels.
Depth: Lower until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor. A good reference is when your elbows touch the tops of your thighs or just inside your knees.
Posture: Ensure your back remains flat and your spine neutral throughout the movement.

Drive: Powerfully drive through your heels to stand up. Use the momentum from your legs to "thrust" the weight upward.
Extension: In one fluid motion, press the bar overhead until your arms are fully extended. At the top, your biceps should be near your ears.
The "Lean": As you reach the top of the press, lean slightly forward into the bar to encourage proper upward rotation of the shoulder blades and avoid lower back arching.

Slowly lower the barbell back to chest height in a controlled manner before immediately beginning the next repetition.

exercises.name: Barbell Step Back Lunge
exercises.description:
Step 1: Stand with your feet hip-width apart, holding a barbell on your upper back.
Step 2: Keep your back straight, chest up, and core engaged.
Step 3: Take a step back with one leg and lower your body by bending both knees. Ensure that your back knee nearly touches the ground.
Step 4: Push off your back foot to return to the starting position.
Step 5: Repeat the movement with the other leg.
Continue alternating between legs for the desired repetitions.

exercises.name: Hammerstrength Decline Chest Press
exercises.description:
Sit upright in a hammerstrength decline chest press machine while squeezing your shoulder blades together and placing your heels firmly on the ground underneath your knees.

The back pad should be contact with your head, shoulders, and butt at all times.

Grab ahold of the handles with an overhand grip just outside shoulder-width apart just below your chest.

Keeping your core braced by breathing into your stomach and flexing the abdominal muscles, push through your palms to extend your elbows while keeping them at a 45 degree angle from your torso.

Once your arms are fully extended, return to the starting position.

exercises.name: External Rotation Stretch
exercises.description:
Sit with your feet pressed against each other, and one knee raised all the way out to the side of your body.

Place your elbow on your raised knee, bend it at 90 degrees, and point your hand directly forward, holding your barbell/dumbbell.

Keep your shoulder depressed and retracted, raise your hand until your forearm is vertical, as if you were about to wave at someone like a robot.

Lower your hand to the original position and repeat.

exercises.name: Incline DB Y-Raise
exercises.description:
Set
an incline bench to a 45-degree angle and sit facing the bench, chest
against the pad, with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other.

Position your feet firmly on the ground for stability and let your arms hang down naturally with a slight bend in your elbows.

Engage your core and keep your back straight throughout the movement.

Raise your arms forward and out to form a Y shape, keeping the movement controlled and your elbows slightly bent.

Lift until your arms are roughly parallel to the floor and in line with your ears.

Pause
briefly at the top of the movement to engage your shoulder muscles
fully, then slowly lower your arms back down to the starting position.

Ensure
the movement is slow and controlled during both the ascent and descent
to maximize engagement of the deltoids and supporting muscles.

Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining proper form throughout.

exercises.name: High-Cable Lateral Raise
exercises.description:
Stand next to a cable machine with the pulley set to waist height.

Grab the opposite-side handle with the hand farthest from the
pulley, keeping your palm facing in.

Keep your core engaged, chest lifted, and shoulders relaxed. Maintain a slight bend in the elbow throughout the lift.

Lift your arm out to the side until your elbow reaches shoulder height, keeping your wrist aligned with your elbow.

Briefly pause at the top, then slowly lower the handle back to your side with control. Repeat for the desired reps.

exercises.name: Shinbox IR Stretch
exercises.description:
Starting Position: Sit on the floor with both hips and knees bent at 90-degree angles.

Leg Placement:
Place one leg in front of you (external rotation) and the other leg out
to the side/behind you (internal rotation). The shins and knees should
remain flat on the ground.

The Movement:
Keeping your hips square, hinge your torso forward or tilt it laterally
(side-to-side) toward the front leg to deepen the stretch.

Target Areas:
Stretches the glutes and piriformis (front leg) and the hip flexors and
quads (back leg). Engages the core and obliques during lateral flexion.

Goal: Improves hip mobility, specifically internal and external rotation, and relieves lower back tension.

exercises.name: YTWL Exercise
exercises.description:
Purpose: Improves shoulder stability, posture, and scapular (shoulder blade) control. Often used in physical therapy and warm-ups.

Starting Position:
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips (like a
deadlift) keeping your back flat, or lie face down on an incline bench.
Keep your thumbs pointing up throughout.

Y (Arms up):
Extend both arms straight forward and upward at a 135-degree angle from
your body, forming a "Y". Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the
top.

T (Arms out): Open your arms straight out to the sides, perpendicular to your body, forming a "T". Focus on pinching your shoulder blades.

W (Arms bent): Pull your elbows back, bending them to 90 degrees, and squeeze your shoulder blades to form a "W". Keep your wrists firm.

L (Arms rotated):
Start with elbows bent at 90 degrees and close to your body. Rotate
your forearms outward (external rotation) like a goalpost, forming an
"L" or a gate.

Key Focus:
Movements should be slow and controlled. Always lead with the thumbs
and think about moving the shoulder blades, not just the arms.

exercises.name: Supine Hip Abduction
exercises.description:
Starting Position:
Lie on your back (supine) on a mat, with your legs extended and
relaxed. Arms can be placed alongside your body or out to the sides for
stability.

The Movement:
Slightly lift one leg off the floor (keeping it straight or with a
slight bend). Move it laterally outward, away from the other leg, as if
stepping over a small obstacle.

Range of Motion:
Move the leg as far as comfortable without lifting your pelvis or
rotating your torso, feeling a stretch in the inner thigh and hip.

Return: Slowly bring the leg back to the starting position with controlled movement.

Goal: Improves lateral hip mobility (abduction) and strengthens the pelvic stabilizer muscles.

exercises.description:
Setup: Lie on a decline bench with your head at the top and grip the handles.

The Start: Extend legs fully, keeping them slightly elevated to engage your core.

The Lift: Raise your legs toward the ceiling using your abs, not momentum.

The Squeeze: Pause and contract your lower abdominals at the top.

The Return: Lower your legs slowly to the starting position with control.

exercises.name: Clean and Press
exercises.description:
The First Pull: Lift the bar from the floor to knee-height by driving with the legs, keeping the angle of your back constant.

The "Power" Position: As the bar reaches mid-thigh, explosively shrug and extend your hips to create vertical momentum.

The Quick Elbow Turnover: In the catch phase, rotate your elbows rapidly under the bar to create a "shelf" on your front deltoids.

The Vertical Press: Press the bar in a straight line; your head should shift slightly forward once the bar clears your forehead to reach full lockout.

exercises.name: Weighted push-ups
exercises.description:
Setup: Begin in a standard plank position with a weight plate balanced securely on your upper back.

Alignment: Maintain a straight line from your head to your heels, engaging your core to prevent your back from sagging.

Execution: Lower your body until your chest nearly touches the floor, keeping your elbows at a forty-five degrees.

Ascent: Press through your palms to return to the starting position, fully extending your arms.

Repeat for reps.

exercises.name: dumbbell snatch
exercises.description:
Key Steps to Execute Correctly:

Setup: Place the dumbbell between your feet, with your shoulders above your hips, chest up, and back flat.

The Pull: Explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles (triple extension) to drive the dumbbell upward, keeping your elbow high and the dumbbell close to your body.

The Catch: Quickly flex your hips and knees to drop under the dumbbell and receive it overhead with your arm locked in position, landing in a half-squat stance.

Common Mistakes: Using your arms too much to lift the weight instead of your legs, having a low elbow during the pull phase, and misaligning your shoulder, elbow, and wrist in the final position. For beginners, it’s recommended to start with light loads, focus on technique, and perform 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps per arm.

exercises.description: This exercise requires a sturdy box or a chair. Simple stand ~6 inches in front of it and balance yourself on one leg. exercises.name: Step Jack
exercises.description:
The Step Jack is a low-impact plyometric-style move that provides cardiovascular benefits without the joint stress of jumping. It works the entire body, specifically targeting the legs, core, and shoulders. This move is ideal for beginners, individuals with joint sensitivities, or as a dynamic warm-up to gradually elevate the heart rate.
Notes (Instructions):

​Stand upright with your feet together and arms at your sides.

​Step your right foot out to the side while simultaneously swinging both arms up above your head.

Bring your right foot back to the center and lower your arms.

​Immediately repeat the movement, stepping out with your left foot.

​Continue alternating sides at a steady, rhythmic pace.

exercises.description:
​A tempo-based squat that uses controlled movement to increase muscle tension and improve lower-body stability.

​Lower: Descend slowly for 3 seconds.

​Pause: Hold at the bottom for 1 second.

​Stand: Return to the starting position at a normal pace.

Form: Keep your chest up and weight in your heels.

​A push-up variation with a wider hand placement to increase the emphasis on the outer chest muscles and shoulders.

​Push: Drive through your palms to return to the start position.

​Form: Don't let your lower back sag; keep a straight line from head to heels.

exercises.name: Single-arm cable pushdown
exercises.description:
Single-arm cable pushdown is a unilateral isolation exercise that targets the triceps brachii. By working one arm at a time, it helps correct strength imbalances between sides while also engaging the core for stability.
Starting position:
Stand facing the cable machine with your feet shoulder-width apart. Attach a single handle to the high pulley. Grab the handle with one hand using an overhand grip (pronated), with your elbow bent at approximately 90° and tucked close to your body. Keep your core braced and your back straight.
Execution:
Push the handle downward in a controlled motion by extending your elbow until your arm is fully extended. Hold the contraction for 1 second at the bottom, then slowly return to the starting position.

exercises.name: Kettlebell sumo high pull
exercises.description:
A compound exercise combining elements of a sumo deadlift and a high pull. It targets the posterior chain, particularly the glutes, hamstrings, and upper back. The sumo stance increases hip engagement, while the high pull adds an explosive element, promoting power development.

Stand upright overtop of a kettlebell with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart angled out slightly.

Maintain a braced core and neutral spine throughout the exercise.

Hinge your hips backward and extend your arms to grab ahold the kettlebell with a double overhand grip.

With you lower legs nearly vertical to the ground, extend your hips to raise the kettlebell with your elbows high keeping it close to your body.

Once the kettlebell has reached shoulder height, lower back to the starting position.

exercises.name: Hip Airplane
exercises.description:
Stand on one leg and lean your upper body slightly forward while keeping your back straight. Extend the free leg behind you so that your torso and leg form roughly one line. Slowly open your hip to the side by rotating your pelvis and upper body in a controlled way. Then close the hip again and return to the starting position.

exercises.name: Curl De Muñeca Con Barra
exercises.description:
This is a variation of the flat bench press designed to emphasize the clavicular head of the pectoralis major (the upper portion). By tilting the torso, the angle of the push changes, shifting more tension to the upper chest and shoulders, which helps achieve a more aesthetic, balanced, and three-dimensional development of the torso.

Starting Position: Grip a bar with an overhand grip (palms facing up) at a width similar to your shoulders.

Position on the Bench: Kneel in front of a flat bench and rest the backs of your forearms on it. Your wrists and hands should extend slightly beyond the edge of the bench to allow for a full range of motion.

Eccentric Phase (Lowering): Lower the bar in a controlled manner by extending your wrists toward the floor. At the bottom of the movement, slightly spread your fingers to let the bar roll down a bit, maximizing the stretch.

Concentric Phase (Lift): First, close your fingers to secure the bar, then flex your wrists upward explosively but in a controlled manner, bringing the bar as high as possible. Strongly contract your forearms at the top position for one second.

Form: Keep your forearms firmly pressed against the bench throughout the exercise; only your wrists and fingers should move.

exercises.name: Bobbing Exhale Drill
exercises.description: Stand in chest-deep water. Take a breath, submerge your face fully, and exhale slowly and completely through your nose and/or mouth the whole time you're underwater — a gentle humming sound can help keep the exhale steady and controlled. Once you're empty of air, lift your head, take a fresh breath, and go back under. Repeat continuously. The goal is training your body that all your exhaling happens underwater, so all you need to do at the surface is inhale.

Extend one leg backwards, resting your foot "laces-down" on the edge of the bench.

Lower yourself until your rear knee is on the floor and you are in a lunge position, with your torso hanging forwards slightly.

Repeat for the other leg, too.

exercises.name: Kegel Exercise
exercises.description:
Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit upright in a chair. Locate the pelvic floor muscles: they are the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or to hold back gas. Keep your abdomen, glutes and thighs relaxed and breathe normally throughout.

Tighten the pelvic floor muscles and lift them gently upwards and inwards. Hold the contraction for a few seconds, then release completely and rest for at least as long as you held. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

The exercise can be varied by holding longer with a light contraction (endurance) or by performing quick, short contractions with a full relaxation in between.

exercises.name: 90/90 Hip Switches
exercises.description:
Sit on the floor with one leg bent at 90 degrees in front of you and the other leg bent at 90 degrees out to the side, so that the rear shin is parallel to the front shin. Keep your torso upright and, if possible, your hands off the floor.

Rotate both knees over to the other side so that the legs swap positions and you arrive in the same 90/90 position facing the opposite way. Move slowly and under control, keeping the feet in contact with the floor, and alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions.

Mobility drill for internal and external rotation of the hips.

exercises.name: Adductor Rock Backs
exercises.description:
Start on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips. Extend one leg straight out to the side with the foot flat on the floor and the toes pointing forward.

Keep your back flat and slowly push your hips back towards the heel of the kneeling leg until you feel a stretch along the inside of the extended leg. Pause briefly, then return to the starting position. Complete all repetitions on one side before switching legs.

Mobility exercise for the adductors and the hips.

exercises.name: Elevated Hamstring Stretch
exercises.description:
Stand facing a bar, box or bench at roughly hip height and place the heel of one leg on it. Keep that leg straight with the toes pointing up, and keep the standing leg straight with both hips square to the support.

Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back until you feel a stretch in the back of the elevated thigh. Hold the position while breathing calmly, then switch legs.

Stretch for the hamstrings. The height of the support controls the intensity: the higher the leg, the stronger the stretch.

exercises.name: Single-leg BOSU balance
exercises.description:
Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise

The exercise for balancing on a BOSU ball while standing on one leg is known as the single-leg BOSU balance exercise. This exercise is effective for enhancing balance, coordination, and core stability.

Benefits of the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise

Improves Balance: Standing on one leg challenges your stability.

Enhances Coordination: Engaging different muscle groups helps improve overall coordination.

Strengthens Core: The exercise activates core muscles, promoting better posture and stability.

How to Perform the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise

Positioning: Stand on the dome side of the BOSU ball with one leg.

Balance: Keep your opposite leg lifted and your core engaged.

Duration: Aim to hold the position for 10-20 seconds, gradually increasing the time as you improve.

Progression Tips

Add Movement: Try reaching for objects around you while maintaining balance.

Close Your Eyes: This increases the challenge by removing visual stability cues.

Use a Ball: Catch or toss a ball while balancing to further engage your core and coordination.

This exercise is a great way to build foundational balance skills before progressing to more complex movements.

exercises.name: Quad Sets
exercises.description:
What Are Quad Sets?

Quad sets are a fundamental exercise used in knee rehabilitation. They focus on strengthening the quadriceps muscles located at the front of the thigh. This exercise is particularly beneficial for individuals recovering from knee injuries or surgeries.

How to Perform Quad Sets
Steps to Execute Quad Sets

Positioning: Sit or lie down with your legs straight.

Tightening: Tighten the quadriceps muscles while keeping the leg straight. You should see the kneecap move upward.

Holding: Maintain the contraction for about 5 seconds.

Releasing: Relax the muscle after the hold.

Repetitions: Aim for 10 to 15 repetitions, gradually increasing as strength improves.

Tips for Effective Quad Sets

Ensure no other muscles are contracting to assist the quadriceps.

Perform the exercise on a flat surface, like a bed or couch, with a towel or pillow under your heel for comfort.

It is recommended to do these exercises multiple times a day, especially during the early stages of recovery.

Benefits of Quad Sets

Restores Muscle Function: Helps rebuild strength in the quadriceps.

Improves Stability: Enhances stability in the knee joint.

Increases Range of Motion: Aids in regaining mobility after injury or surgery.

Incorporating quad sets into your rehabilitation routine can significantly aid in recovery and improve overall knee function.

exercises.name: Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps
exercises.description:
Overview of Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps

Hip-out and hip-in lateral steps are effective exercises designed to strengthen the hip abductors and enhance lateral stability. These movements are beneficial for improving coordination and overall hip function.

Exercise Descriptions
Hip-Out Steps

Movement: Step out to the side with one leg, keeping the other leg stable.

Target Muscles: Primarily engages the hip abductors, including the gluteus medius and minimus.

Benefits: Increases lateral stability and strength in the hip area.

Hip-In Steps

Movement: Bring the leg back in toward the center after stepping out.

Target Muscles: Continues to engage the hip abductors while also activating the adductors.

Benefits: Enhances coordination and control of the hip joint.

Key Benefits of Lateral Steps

| Benefit | Description |
|---|---|
| Strengthening Hip Abductors | Improves muscle strength around the hip joint. |
| Enhancing Stability | Increases lateral stability, reducing the risk of falls. |
| Improving Coordination | Develops better control and movement patterns in the hips. |

Incorporating hip-out and hip-in lateral steps into a regular exercise routine can lead to improved hip strength and stability, which is essential for various physical activities and daily movements.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
exercises.description:
Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises that focus on balance and stability by landing softly on one leg and holding the position. This exercise helps improve proprioception and can be beneficial for rehabilitation and athletic training.

Overview

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises designed to enhance balance, stability, and proprioception. They involve landing softly on one leg and maintaining that position for a brief period. This exercise is particularly useful in rehabilitation settings and for athletes looking to improve their performance.

Benefits

Improves balance: Enhances stability by training the body to control weight distribution on one leg.

Enhances proprioception: Increases awareness of body position, which is crucial for injury prevention.

Supports rehabilitation: Helps individuals recover from lower-limb injuries by strengthening muscles and improving joint stability.

How to Perform Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
Steps

Preparation: Stand on a stable surface or a box.

Takeoff: Step off the box or surface with one leg, ensuring that you do not jump.

Landing: Land softly on the target leg, allowing the knee and hip to bend slightly.

Hold position: Maintain balance in the landed position for up to 2 seconds.

Reset: Return to the starting position and repeat.

Key Points to Remember

Keep your chest up and engage your core for better stability.

Ensure your knee aligns with the midline of your foot during landing.

Focus on a controlled descent to minimize impact.

Conclusion

Incorporating single-leg soft-landing holds into your training routine can significantly enhance your balance and stability, making it a valuable exercise for both rehabilitation and athletic performance.

exercises.name: Reverse V-Squat
exercises.description:
Step into the V-squat machine facing the pad, the opposite way from the regular V-squat, so that your chest rests against the pad and your shoulders sit under the shoulder pads. Place your feet on the platform about shoulder width apart and release the safety.

Brace your core and lower yourself by bending your knees and pushing the hips back until your thighs are roughly parallel to the platform. Drive back up through the heels without locking out the knees.

Compared to the regular V-squat, the reversed position shifts the emphasis towards the glutes and hamstrings.

exercises.name: Seated Band Row
exercises.description: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you and your back tall. Loop a resistance band around the soles of both feet and hold one end in each hand, arms extended and a slight bend in the knees. Pull the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows straight back and squeezing your shoulder blades together. Keep your chest up and your torso still rather than rocking backward to move the band. Extend the arms slowly to return. Because the torso stays upright and supported, this is a useful row when a bent-over position is uncomfortable, and it needs no anchor point.

exercises.name: FlexBar Wrist Extension
exercises.description: Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing down and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist drop, then extend the wrist to raise the bar, keeping the forearm still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. The resistance comes from twisting or bending the flexible bar, so a thicker or stiffer bar increases the load. Commonly used for wrist and forearm strengthening and for elbow tendon rehabilitation.

exercises.description: An eccentric exercise for the wrist extensors, done with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar, and widely used in rehabilitation for lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). Hold the bar vertically in the affected hand with the wrist extended. Grasp the top of the bar with the other hand, palm facing away, and twist the top hand to wind up the bar. Bring both arms out in front of you with the bar horizontal, then slowly let the affected wrist untwist the bar over about four seconds while the other hand holds steady. Reset and repeat. The reverse version, twisting in the opposite direction for the wrist flexors, is used for medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Move slowly and stop if the exercise causes sharp pain rather than the expected mild discomfort.

exercises.name: Seated Knee Extension with Overpressure
exercises.description: A gentle stretch to restore full knee extension. Sit with one leg stretched out in front of you and the heel propped on the floor or a low surface, so the knee is unsupported. Place both hands on the thigh just above the kneecap. Keeping the leg relaxed, gently press down through the hands toward the floor until you feel a stretch behind the knee, and hold for about three seconds before releasing. The pressure should produce a stretch, never sharp pain. Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then switch legs.

exercises.name: Banded Monster Walk
exercises.description: A banded walking drill for the glutes and hip stabilisers. Place a mini band around both thighs just above the knees, or around the ankles for a harder version. Stand with feet hip-width apart so the band is under tension, then sink into a quarter-squat with the chest up. Walk forward with small diagonal steps, pushing each leg out against the band and keeping the knees tracking over the toes rather than letting them fall inward. Walk forward for the prescribed number of steps, then walk backward to return, keeping the band under tension throughout.

exercises.name: Step Calf Stretch
exercises.description: Stand on a step or a sturdy raised surface with the balls of both feet on the edge and the heels hanging off, holding a rail or wall for balance. Let one or both heels drop below the level of the step until you feel a stretch through the calf, and hold. Keep the knee straight to stretch the gastrocnemius, or bend the knee slightly to bias the soleus lower down. Hold for the prescribed time, typically 30 seconds, without bouncing, then switch sides if stretching one leg at a time.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Balance with Eyes Closed
exercises.description: A balance and proprioception drill. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent and the other foot lifted clear of the floor, then close your eyes and hold the position. Without visual feedback the ankle and hip stabilisers have to do the work, so expect noticeable wobble. Stand within reach of a wall, counter or chair so you can steady yourself if needed. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch legs. Commonly prescribed in rehabilitation after ankle or knee injury.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Balance with Kettlebell Circles
aliases: Kettlebell Body Circle on One Leg
exercises.description: A balance drill that adds a moving load. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent, holding a kettlebell in one hand. Pass the kettlebell around your body in a circle, handing it from one hand to the other in front and behind you, while keeping your balance on the standing leg. Keep the hips level and the torso upright; the shifting weight of the bell constantly changes your centre of mass, which is what trains the hip and ankle stabilisers. Complete the prescribed number of circles, reverse direction, then switch legs. Use a light bell to start.

exercises.name: Bent Over Dumbbell Rows (Two Arms)
exercises.description:
How to Perform It

Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral or overhand grip.

Hinge at the hips, pushing your glutes back, until your torso is roughly 45–75 degrees to the floor. Keep a slight bend in your knees.

Let the dumbbells hang directly below your shoulders with arms fully extended.

Keep your back flat, chest up, and core braced — avoid rounding your spine.

Pull the dumbbells up toward your ribcage/hips, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top.

Pause briefly at the top of the movement.

Lower the dumbbells back down under control to the starting position.

Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Key Coaching Cues

Hinge from the hips, not the lower back

Keep the spine neutral throughout — no rounding

Lead with the elbows, not the hands

Avoid using momentum or jerking the weight up

Control the eccentric (lowering) phase rather than letting the weights drop

exercises.name: Radio Taiso
exercises.description:
Video can be found here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGPBSqxKGAc

Full-body mobility and dynamic warm-up routine (3–5 minutes) to prepare joints, muscles, and the cardiovascular system for workout.

Movement Flow:

Deep Breathing & Arm Raises: Inhale while raising arms laterally overhead, exhale as you lower them.

Knee Bends: Soft, rhythmic knee flexions synchronized with arm swings.

Arm Circles: Large full-range arm rotations forward, then backward to open up the chest and shoulder girdle.

Chest Expansion: Cross arms in front of the chest and open wide to the sides.

Side Bends: Reach overhead to stretch the lateral torso left and right with a smooth side flexion.

Forward & Back Bends: Gently hinge at the hips to reach forward, then return upright with a mild spinal extension.

Torso Twists: Swing arms side-to-side to rotate the spine and loosen the core.

Ankle Mobility / Light Bounces: Soft heel lifts or light bouncing on toes to warm up lower leg joints and tendons.

exercises.name: kelso shrugs
exercises.description:
Kelso shrugs are a variation of scapular shrugs designed primarily to train scapular retraction, with particular emphasis on the middle trapezius, rhomboids, and, secondarily, the lower trapezius. Unlike conventional shrugs, the goal is not to elevate the shoulders toward the ears, but rather to pull the shoulder blades backward.

They are typically performed with the chest supported on an incline bench, using either dumbbells or a barbell:

Lie face down on an incline bench, with your arms extended toward the floor.

Keep your elbows almost completely locked throughout the movement.

Starting with the shoulder blades slightly protracted, retract them, trying to bring them closer together.

Keep your chest firmly supported on the bench; avoid turning the movement into a row by extending your torso.

Briefly hold the fully retracted position, then return in a controlled manner, allowing the shoulder blades to separate.

exercises.name: Stomach Vacuum
exercises.description:
Starting position: Lie flat on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor (or stand/sit upright).

Exhalation: Fully exhale all the air from your lungs through your mouth.

Contraction: Draw your navel in towards your spine as far as possible, pulling your stomach inward and up under your ribcage.

Hold: Hold this isometric contraction without breathing for 10 to 20 seconds.

Release: Slowly inhale through your nose to release the tension and relax your abdominals.

Repeat: Rest briefly and perform the desired number of sets.

exercises.name: Tyson push-ups
exercises.description:
Starting Position

• Feet: Place the soles of your feet flat against a vertical wall, with your toes or balls of your feet on the floor.
• Hands: Position your hands on the floor shoulder-width apart, directly under your lower chest or solar plexus.
• Body: Keep your core tight, glutes squeezed, and head in a neutral position. Your knees should hover a few inches above the floor without touching it.

Movement Pattern

Lower Down: Flex your elbows (tucked around 45 degrees) to lower your chest toward the floor, stopping just a few centimeters short of touching the ground.

Rock Back: As you press upward through your arms, push your hips backward and bend your knees, rocking your weight toward your heels while keeping your shins nearly parallel to the floor.

Drive Forward: Explode forward from your lower-body/crouched position, shifting your weight back into the starting push-up plank stance to complete the repetition.

Key Tips for Proper Form

• Keep Knees Low: Do not let your knees or hips pike high up in the air; keep the motion low and horizontal.
• Maintain Wall Contact: Keep the soles of your feet pressed against the wall so you don't lose your leverage.
• Engage the Core: Avoid arching your lower back by tilting your pelvis backward and bracing your abs.

exercises.name: Dumbbell single arm row
exercises.description:
Place a dumbbell next to a flat bench

Place your left knee on on the bench, and plant your left hand on the bench so it is under your shoulder.

Place your right foot on the floor in line with your left knee

Grab the dumbbell with your right hand, neutral grip.

Starting position, shoulders should be in line and back paraller to the floor

Slowly pull the dumbbell up, by pushing your elbow upwards, keeping it close to your body.

Do repeats on one side, then on the other.

exercises.name: Hamstring Stretch
exercises.description: Sit on the floor. Extend your right leg straight out in front of you. Bend your left leg and place the sole of your left foot against the inner side of your right thigh (with your knee pointing to the side). Straighten your upper body completely (chest out, shoulders back). Inhale, and as you exhale, bend forward from the hips (not the lower back!) over your extended right leg. Reach for your shin, ankle, or foot—whichever is possible while keeping your back straight.

exercises.name: V-Up - Mark Lauren
exercises.description:
One of the best exercises for the rectus abdominis muscles. Lie on your back with your legs straight and your arms close to your sides. Lift your head off the floor and raise your legs and arms about 15 centimeters off the floor. Your palms should face down, and look up at the ceiling.
Now bend your legs and at the same time sit up so that your knees and chest almost touch. Only your buttocks are still on the floor. Your arms are now extended at shoulder height. Then slowly return to the starting position with your arms and legs extended and your head raised.

exercises.name: Active Hang
exercises.description: A static hold from a pull-up bar with straight elbows and actively depressed, stabilized shoulders. Grip a secure bar and let your body hang under control. Keep your elbows straight and gently draw your shoulders down, away from your ears. Maintain this active shoulder position without pulling up, swinging, or repeatedly moving the shoulder blades. Hold for up to 30 seconds. Stop earlier if your grip opens, shoulder control deteriorates, or pain occurs. Record actual seconds, grip, and any assistance used. This is distinct from a relaxed passive dead hang or a moving scapular pull-up.

exercises.name: Pike Hold (Floor)
exercises.description: A static bodyweight support with both hands and feet on the floor and hips raised in a pike position. Place your hands and feet securely on the floor, then raise your hips. Keep your elbows straight and actively push the floor away through your shoulders. Maintain a controlled, stationary position without bending your elbows, lowering your head for push-up repetitions, or raising your feet onto a surface. Hold for up to 30 seconds. Stop earlier for loss of alignment, loss of active shoulder support, or pain. Record actual seconds, hand and foot spacing, and alignment. This is the floor variation, not a pike push-up or an elevated-feet pike hold.
